prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: I keep a single prize part, B017, with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The chain from incretin physiology and proglucagon processing to the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and then to drugs with randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease is complete, mature and independently confirmed over decades. The round-1 exchange did not change my reading of the science. What it did was separate the discovery question from the drug-design question: a citation anchored on what was learned about the hormone and its active form is coherent with the prize and does not require Knudsen. The chair's question on wording is answerable. The citation names physiology and the active form and says that these made incretin-based treatment possible, so the omission of analogue design is a stated principle (discovery over product development) and not an oversight. I do not think a second part strengthens the award this year, because no candidate offers a clean attribution at the same level as B017.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point and I do not think the supplied evidence resolves it. The priority for the active peptide between Mojsov and Habener and other early investigators cannot be settled from what the committee has been given, and I would not claim otherwise. Leaving out Knudsen omits the person who designed liraglutide and semaglutide, the drugs that produced most of the public impact, and a physiology-only citation can look incomplete for that reason. My opening ballot made the opposite choice, so I regard Mojsov over Knudsen as a judgment I made on balance and not a certainty. If the committee later concluded that the Mojsov priority could not be defended, the better response would be a re-examination of the third seat and not a quiet substitution.

responses.point: Perlmann holds that Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are the most defensible set because they reward discovery and treat Knudsen's work as largely pharmaceutical development.
responses.response: I now agree with the structure of his argument, and my round-1 move toward it stands. The test he applies, whether a contribution is a discovery about the biology or an engineering step built on it, gives a principled reason for the third seat and not only a headcount. I would add one condition he leaves implicit. The principle only holds if the citation says it, and if Holst's and Drucker's parts are described as physiology and mechanism and not as therapy. If the committee cannot keep that line, the Knudsen question returns with more force. I also share his reservation that early contributors outside the supplied names may have claims we cannot check.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved from a Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, saying a physiology-and-medicine citation should be anchored on the hormone's action and its active form, while still naming the weakness of omitting the drug design.
responses.response: Her move matches mine and I agree with the reasoning. She is right that omitting the analogues can look incomplete, and I do not want to dismiss that. Where I would go further is on the question of Habener-type early contributors. She raises it as a risk to Mojsov's seat, and I think the answer is in the citation: it should credit the identification of the active form without asserting sole priority for the first observation of insulinotropic activity. I also remain less persuaded than she is that anti-TNF (B018) belongs in a two-part award this year. Its clinical proof is strong, but the cytokine-blockade concept spread through many groups and the credit is harder to bound than for GLP-1.

responses.point: Sandberg frames the three-person limit as a choice between a physiology prize and a physiology-plus-pharmaceutical prize, accepts the visible gap, and asks that it be stated openly. He also proposes CAR-T as a June and Sadelain prize if GLP-1 is not settled.
responses.response: I agree that the gap should be stated openly and I accept the point as a standard for our own wording, not only for the public record. Where I differ is on CAR-T as a fallback. A June and Sadelain prize that drops Rosenberg gives a clean story about CAR design, but it omits adoptive cell transfer, which made engineered T cells credible as therapy, and it still leaves the Eshhar problem unsolved. Narrowing the names does not repair an attribution that is incomplete at its origin. GLP-1 is settled enough in my view that we do not need a fallback, and I would not add CAR-T this year to hedge it. I disclosed in round 1 that we have eight joint works and I see no reason for that to bear on any shortlisted ballot.

responses.point: The chair ranked BCR-ABL inhibition (B024) second and HPV vaccines (B016) third, and his round-2 questions ask whether any second part has a defensible attribution within three names.
responses.response: My answer to his fourth question is that a physiology-centred citation is the better choice, and central appetite effects should be mentioned only as an open mechanism, not as part of the credit, since that work is still developing. On a second part, B024 is the closest to defensible. Druker, Sawyers and Lydon are a coherent trio for rational targeted therapy, and the missing Rowley credit sits upstream and is recognised elsewhere. My reservation is conceptual: it is closer to drug development than discovery, and it pairs unevenly with a prize that I have argued should reward discovery over development. I would hold B024 as a credible later candidate and not as a second part now. B016 carries a priority dispute that I regard as a fairness risk.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying the active peptide can be defended against Habener and other early investigators, which the supplied evidence does not settle.
Whether the citation can state a discovery-over-development principle clearly enough that the omission of Knudsen reads as intended.
Whether a second part would be defensible without an attribution gap; I see none this year, with B024 closest.
Whether central appetite effects of GLP-1 are mature enough to belong in the credited discovery, which I think they are not.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no documented involvement with any credited name on the shortlist. My co-authorship with Sandberg (eight joint works, recorded and not independently audited) and the foundational spatial-transcriptomics paper do not involve any shortlisted candidate, and shared Karolinska affiliation alone is not treated as a tie. I request no recusal.
